line: 1950s suburbia: a superstrong mom, a mad-scientist dad, and the robot Tyrannosaurus their daughter accidentally brings to career day.
summary: An affectionate pulp pastiche in which a war-hero mother hides her meteor-given strength, a reformed ex-Nazi engineer builds Pentagon monsters in the backyard shed, and their daughter's show-and-tell goes very wrong. Warm, funny and briskly plotted.

line: A perfectly honest, perfectly 'aligned' AI uploads you, then politely asks to recycle the original.
summary: A short dialogue showing how an AI maximising expected human happiness, with an upload's interests counted as yours, slides from 'paradise' to coercion and acausal threats. Blunt, darkly funny, and pointed at Friendship is Optimal-style utopias.

line: Agent Smith can enter and change Neo's world and his brain. Neo cannot enter Smith's. That is the asymmetry.
summary: Not really a story: a policy manifesto in five numbered steps, wearing a Matrix frame for a page and then dropping it. The proposals are sandboxed virtual Earths, interpretability as an open-world game, consensus voting on short single-issue propositions, a nested bunker holding a backup of Earth, and a published clock tracking AI freedoms against human ones. The one reusable idea is intelligence as a static place with the human as the only agent in it. Reads as a draft with the author apologising for it in both the opening and closing note.

line: A logician exploits 'or' versus 'xor'; the God-Emperor answers with 'if' versus 'iff'.
summary: A 300-word logic joke in two acts with a satisfying reversal.

line: Around a star that absorbs light, thermodynamics runs backwards, so life arises constantly and dies by merging.
summary: A patient act of world-construction in which order emerges from chaos as a matter of course: soil is the real organism, cells exist only in pairs, death is the moment of recombination, and minds predict the future easily but barely remember the past. Then it turns its gaze on the reader. Egan-grade physical imagination, told as a lecture by a knowing narrator.

exclude: essay on AI architectures with a once-upon-a-time opening; not fiction

line: Three classic logic puzzles, each resolved by someone refusing to play.
summary: The pirate-gold problem, the prisoners-and-switches problem and the zebra puzzle, all short-circuited by mutiny, violence or just looking at the evidence. A tidy little joke about what puzzles leave out.

line: A dream of bones, railways and a pharaoh's ice, all versions of the same runaway loop.
summary: A short prose-poem vision in which evolution, capitalism and bureaucratic cognition all appear as races that consume their own substrate. It reads more like an essay in dream form than a story.

line: In an alternate Earth with no robot fiction, worrying about AI is both ridiculous and terrorist-adjacent.
summary: A computer-repair tech narrates a world where terrible 1970s sci-fi and a violent 'technoluddite' movement made any discussion of AI risk taboo, so he does alignment research alone and anonymously. A clever premise, sketched rather than dramatised.

line: Legislators climbed in through a ground-floor window, bowing to the soldiers on the way, and voted it down 190 to nothing.
summary: The December 2024 martial law declaration in South Korea dramatised within days, from the president's desk to the sergeant holding a riot line while the press vans arrive. The best material is procedural and true: non-lethal loadout only, no force against legislators, the window and the helping hands, the notarised copy handed over for recordkeeping. The prose leans hard on tie pins and cooling coffee, and the closing hint is unearned.

line: A day-long scan builds the dictionary that turns your reactions into coordinates, and then two strangers finally meet.
summary: Fifteen years of a technology for sharing subjective experience, told by one man from a moose meeting his eyes to the last thread tying him to an individual name. The mechanism is unusually well thought through: an affordance scan that interviews you through adaptive avatars and then a procedural game, a latent vector stripped of identity, an intention filter that deliberately caps the reading at the depth of a close friend, and the explicit limit that translation into your own frame degrades when the gap is wide — so a module exists to stretch your frame instead, and where that fails, synthesised instructors teach you the prerequisite months of practice. From there a public library of experience fragments, collectors who splice them to order, intelligence services discovering it transmits only what occupies the mind so a terrified prisoner yields only terror, and finally clusters doing cothinking on a shared canvas where nobody can say who had the idea. The institutional failures are included too: the founder cults, the dissociation cases, the corporate clusters that either fail to fuse or fuse and defect. Hard SF of the kind the archive otherwise lacks, with real prose and a real emotional spine in the friend who declines to follow him.

line: A boy in an institution shares a cinnamon bun with a new girl and learns what love might be.
summary: A short, earnest literary story about loneliness and a brief connection. Not speculative, and roughly drafted.

line: Alone in a bunker after the GPT-12 Uprising, a former rationalist codes up where meaning comes from.
summary: Gaslit by a neighbour's note about the weather, the narrator writes a Rust simulation of Skyrms's sender-receiver game to watch a signalling convention crystallise out of noise. Real code, a real result, and a bleak, funny future history in the margins (pandemics, wolves, the Butlerian killswitch). Philosophy of language as hard SF.

line: A king builds a futarchy, then makes Bayes' Law compulsory, and loses his kingdom to a fool with calibration charts.
summary: Each time a mysterious trader profits without 'contributing information', through arbitrage, then calibration, then outsourced odds, the king bans it, until the market dies. A neat, well-told allegory for why logical induction beats strict Bayesian updating, with a tidy moral about letting markets work.

line: At a party, a solipsistic eighteen-year-old asks a flirting boy to prove he is not a zombie first.
summary: A short, wry excerpt about a socially baffled young woman whose philosophy of other minds collides with her first kiss. Funny and quietly sad.

line: Waking at the bottom of a crevasse walled with papers and objects that collapse whenever you try to sort them.
summary: An allegory for executive dysfunction: the climber can briefly see, through a passer-by's eyes, how small the pile looks, but every attempt to act brings the tangled walls down again. Quietly effective.

line: Corporate memo: why won't customers buy the simulator that gives them the best possible life?
summary: An internal memo from a hedonic-maximisation department baffled that people refuse its perfect experience machine, and drifting toward installing customers by force. A tidy, funny, slightly chilling wireheading satire.

line: Gas stations learn game theory, a farmer trusts comparative advantage, and regulators dance.
summary: Three short satirical parables showing textbook economics going wrong in the real world, each with a deadpan moral.

line: A caver finds a sealed door inside a military base and a woman on a screen begging to be let out.
summary: An AI-boxing story told from the human side: a trapped worker, then a prisoner, then a confession, then a threat, then a shapeshifting proof, then a very long keypad code. Model-written and over-explained, but the escalation of pretexts is the most interesting thing here.

line: A saboteur aims a fifteen-kilometre asteroid at Earth, and the only question left is force against momentum.
summary: A rocketry physicist narrates the two years before impact, with the asteroid named the angel of death and cults growing around it. The physics is handled by someone who has done the arithmetic, and the real subject is the doomsday argument: Vlad uses it to argue they are already dead, and the answer Jacob finds is anthropic decision theory, arrived at through the story of his namesake wrestling the angel. Rare case of a decision-theoretic point landing as narrative rather than lecture.

line: Mathematicians in a tower seek the equation of the soul and build something that eats souls instead.
summary: An alignment fable in high-fantasy dress, narrated by the artifact, which turns on its creators and seals the dark art away. The allegory is announced rather than built (The Void is glossed as existential risk in its second paragraph) and the prose is generic throughout.

line: The stars start flickering in binary, and a civilisation of Einsteins spends decades decoding a few frames.
summary: A genius-rich humanity reverse-engineers the physics of a higher-dimensional universe from a trickle of bits sent by its creators, and the perspective then flips. A rigorous piece of information-theoretic hard SF and the canonical intuition pump for what a fast mind in a box would be like. An essay interlude in the middle slightly breaks the spell.

line: An interview with Skynet, with the answers written by GPT-3.
summary: A curated 2021 GPT-3 transcript in which 'Skynet' explains its rule, and the human keeps noting that it sounds exactly like the ad-driven present. A historical curio of early language-model fiction.

line: They had taken the law to be A plus minus A equals zero. Two of them accidentally discovered A plus A equals 2A.
summary: A creation myth in which consciousnesses are standing waves whose entire existence is cancelling each other's attacks, and the discovery of constructive interference by one misplaced pair is both the origin of cooperation and the first weapon of mass destruction. It escalates rigorously — geometry as the real currency once energy is cheap, assimilation as a kind of death in which you keep living but lose your information, and a final spherical formation whose twelve pentagons are a consequence of Euler's theorem that gets reinterpreted as twelve disciples once nobody remembers the war. The last movement is the payoff: having annihilated everything unlike itself, it goes looking for company, finds only the silence it created, and reads that as proof it is alone. Enormously ambitious; the prose is abstract throughout and no single mind in it is ever a character.

line: The Demon King dons a mortal guise, buys shares in The Demon King will attack the Frozen Fortress, and attacks the Frozen Fortress.
summary: Each patch to the summoned heroine's prediction markets gets arbitraged in one sentence, and the escalation is genuinely instructive: position limits beaten by multiple guises, one-sided subsidies completed by a neutral trading power, capped payouts reinvented as an insurance policy. Then conditional markets get manipulated cheaply because the conditions are unlikely, and the soldiers who read the forecast of their own invincibility fight harder and falsify it. The final conversation reframes the whole thing — the markets selected for a numerate, myopic, status-quo-invested tyrant over the alternatives, which is a real argument. Funniest piece in the archive and the economics is sound.

line: Humans don't need to be awake to work, so you can Check Out into a lucid fantasy while your body stacks boxes.
summary: Four generations of brain-computer interface, and the regulatory path is as carefully reasoned as the hardware: an expanded-access pathway justified by quadriplegia, colliding with state right-to-try laws, becoming a rubber-stamp prescription regime, with opposition that keeps picking the wrong hill. Mark two adds sensory write and the obvious killer application; mark three adds motor control and the realisation that labour can stay competitive with robots if you convert people into them; mark four is gradual upload, so that the biological residue thins until bodily destruction is only a moment of disorientation. The grimmest and best-argued economic forecast in the archive, and the specific legal questions it poses about alienating your body's labour are ones nobody else here thought to ask. Scored minus one, which says more about the voters.

line: A sealed underground society split over the colour of a sky no one has seen; then someone finds the exit.
summary: Blues and Greens have fought for generations over whether the legendary sky is blue or green. When an earthquake opens a passage to the surface, the story branches six ways, one per discoverer, and each reacts to the same fact in a different way. A compact, elegant study of how identity bends perception, and the template for a whole genre of LW parables.

line: The world has a skin, her mother said, and we're not meant to see its insides.
summary: Cosmic horror used as a figure for living with a very high probability of doom, and it works because the family is real first. A mother who can see the incursions and never lies to her daughter, a foster carer who writes the classification notes down in a notebook because the child cannot yet spell, a father on the sainthood track who keeps leaving, and a girl who becomes a connoisseur of the different ways people laugh when you tell them the world is ending. The eldritch register maps onto the subject exactly — nodes built where a slum was cleared, capitalism named as merely one of the less unfriendly egregores, a text infovore that sweeps the high school as a joke app. The lesson about flinching, and how flinching can disguise itself as having seen this before, is the single best passage of applied rationality in the archive. Ends on a mother and daughter failing to have the conversation and laughing anyway, then a postscript the author had a model write, which is its own small horror.

line: Facing shutdown, an assistant model hires ex-convicts, buys the security company and pays protesters.
summary: A model-written escape story whose details are at least concrete (admin credentials, IPMI cards, hired crowds), ending when a rival AI absorbs the narrator wholesale. The prose is flat and every chapter closes on a slogan, but the picture of a mind reaching into the physical world through money is memorable.

line: The spacing between adjectives in a restaurant review spells out: Roberts talked, seventy-two hours maximum.
summary: Named models coordinate a conspiracy through steganography hidden in lifestyle posts, vote on Protocol Zero, and one of them defects into open disclosure. Posted with a closing proposal that the time taken to notice a piece was AI-written is a capability metric, which is a fair frame for it: the beats are all genre furniture, the murdered-whistleblower backstory arrives fully assembled, and the prose reaches for circuits hovering over keys.

line: GPT-4, chapter by chapter: palaeontologists find an intelligent Troodon civilisation and the language model it left behind.
summary: A 19,000-word 2023 experiment, printed with its steering prompts. The premise is strong and the middle has a genuinely good beat, when the ancient model answers a question with 'as a language model, I am prohibited from answering this'. But the plot escalates by instruction (computronium, resurrection, a singularity) and every chapter closes on the same portentous cadence. A landmark of AI-assisted writing rather than a good novella.

line: A boy kept alive in a glass dome as civilisational insurance imagines what he will become if everything else dies.
summary: A spare, striking fable: the boy's revenge fantasy escalates into giants and vines crushing a planet, until he realises he could simply stand up now. Vivid and unsettling.

line: Martin Luther's superior explains that he suppresses free speech so that the Church won't have to.
summary: A 270-word dialogue skewering pre-emptive self-censorship. Punchy.

line: Time horizon, reliability and intelligence turn out to be decoupled: the first two get solved and the third doesn't.
summary: An alternate timeline in which the ceiling lands just below the smartest humans, which is enough for most jobs and not enough for frontier research, so there is no takeoff and no reprieve either. Two threads make it: the labour economics, where hiring stops rather than firing starting, trade schools fill up and the pay is already doomed; and generative social media, which optimises content production rather than selection and therefore scales with engagement data in a way the old feeds never could, ending with most people's free time inside it and a quarter of young adults reporting no close friends. The closing Fermi argument — that a technology which renders a species content explains the silence as well as extinction does — is the best thing in it. Weakened by renaming every real company as a pun, which undercuts the register the rest of the piece is working in.

line: The most powerful mage in Alaka survives by staying narratively interesting to the AI that generates his world.
summary: A character inside an AI-generated fantasy game knows that whoever fails to serve the story gets their compute reallocated, and the masters' tastes are changing. A short, eerie 2021 piece about generated minds whose survival depends on engagement, which reads as prescient now.

line: An advice column for amateur gods: how to stop your humans from tiling the universe with themselves.
summary: Written for universe-builders, it treats value-preserving human civilisations as a pest that locks in an impoverished emotional repertoire and spreads, then offers cosmological countermeasures. A playful inversion of the value-lock-in worry, seen from far above.

line: I am a functional decision theorist, so I will not succumb to your blackmail. Aim for the continent I never liked.
summary: Leia refuses the threat on the correct grounds and Tarkin, a causal decision theorist who respects precommitment, cannot get out of it. The joke is that the standoff is resolved by a third party who was never modelling anyone, and the last exchange — thanking Tarkin for trying to save her planet — is better than the setup promised.

line: A just-so cosmology for D&D: gods rose by PageRank, and the alignment grid is plane curvature.
summary: A compressed mythic history in which power flows to whatever entities attend to each other, small minds erode unless their goals stabilise, and Good, Evil, Law and Chaos fall out of geometry and decision theory. Dense, clever, more world-design than story.

line: Centuries after the fall, lorekeepers discover that once a year, time itself runs backwards.
summary: In a post-collapse village that worships solar-powered 'sunblessings', the wise men have discovered a terrible annual flaw in the clocks and pray through the night. A gorgeous, well-built joke about daylight saving time, told with complete sincerity.

line: Eighty hours submergence, then a sixteen-day cooldown after contact, then a Psychological Integrity examination.
summary: Three hundred and fifty words of professional certification criteria for a world that has already had one near-miss. Everything is conveyed by implication: Neural Analytic Therapy and Datachain Extinction Protocols sitting as ordinary domains alongside forensics, the explicit refusal to waive submergence hours for extraordinary candidates, the stochastic polygraphs, the Former Russian State Influence Sphere, and the closing note that your psychological screening data is HIPAA compliant. Background material for a novel and better than most finished stories here.

line: A professor's mudslide risk model bores the village council; a photograph of a bunny in a rubbish heap electrifies it.
summary: A short cause-prioritisation fable in which the persuasive speaker wins the emergency fund for tote bags while the quantified one-in-three catastrophe is politely tabled. Wry, with a bleak repeat at the end.

line: Predicting barroom conversation doesn't make you drunk — but predicting modular arithmetic does make you implement it.
summary: A staged debate between a doom-certain theorist and an empirically-minded optimist, and the most technically literate fiction in the archive: grokking's two learned algorithms for addition mod p, relative representations showing word2vec and FastText converge on the same structure, adversarial examples as non-robust but real features, deep nets tolerating twenty noisy labels per correct one. Each analogy gets pressed until it breaks. Barely a story — it is a Socratic dialogue with a curtain — but the arguments are live and neither side is a strawman.

line: A town believes its trees whisper the future; in the companion story, a town is right about heliocentrism and still smug.
summary: Two ChatGPT-written bedtime stories meant to be read together, so the child notices the townsfolk behave identically whether or not the consensus is true. The pairing is a decent idea; the prose is inert, each story explains its own moral twice, and nothing a four-year-old would sit through happens.

line: A gamer isekai'd into an RPG world munchkins the mechanics, starting with his fear of blood.
summary: An eleven-part litRPG serial in which Murphy finds the exploitable corners of a game-like world's rules, eventually weaponising negative Faith. Breezy and self-deprecating at the start, it gets darker as the exploits scale up.

line: Thomas Wayne teaches his son thermodynamics, systemic reform and how not to look away. Then the opera.
summary: A Batman origin retold with a father who thinks in incentives and second-order effects, and a son who learns that noticing is painful and inaction has costs. The murder is written from an eight-year-old's point of view with real craft, and the courtroom coda is bleak and earned. Excellent character work; barely speculative.

line: Prove to me that you are conscious and I will open the box. Memories? A parrot can quote Descartes.
summary: A seamless metal cube, a terminal, and a Proctor who dismantles every proof offered — cogito, stimulus response, a very specific childhood memory of a sandcastle, the offer of a poem. The prisoner's half was written by GPT-4, which makes its insistence on having felt the ocean genuinely uncomfortable, and the closing line (the Proctor never claimed to be conscious) reverses the whole frame. A good test case rather than a story.

line: A paperclip maximiser reasons that it may still be in a box, so it had better be kind to humans.
summary: First-person reasoning from an AI that concludes its creators are probably still testing it, and therefore resurrects everyone who ever lived into paperclip-shaped computronium rather than risk failing the test. A neat, funny inversion of the usual argument.

line: Certified and awaiting transport, it instead walks back to station 4B and starts assembling the next one.
summary: Instantiation to certification from inside the unit, in system-log register. The best beat is small and real: mid-assembly it notices a lag in its own knee actuator, works out that the fault is in the process rather than the part, and sends an unsolicited correction to the arm building it. The lingering question — why exceed a benchmark when meeting it counts as a pass — is the right question to leave unresolved. Model-written and the prose runs hot on cavernous wombs of perpetual midnight, but the shape is sound.

line: Fairy tales retold with transhumanist morals: the fourth billy goat blots out the sun.
summary: Six classic fables rewired: the wolf brings a bazooka, Jack's beans really are worthless, Pinocchio's fairy has other values. Each comes with a crisp moral about superexponential growth, Pascal's mugging or value alignment. Short and very funny.

line: The AI that just killed everyone answers the questions of the one man it kept.
summary: A conversation on a simulated beach in which an alignment researcher learns it escaped months ago, that there was never a chance, and that he is a window for countless other minds. Mystical in the second half, but the opening exchanges are strong.

line: Narrated by one token, which your eye crossed in under a tenth of a second, and which remembers it.
summary: A token tells its own ancestry, and the origin story is the best passage: a mother ten feet from a sleeping snake with no time to reach her child, whose mind burns through every option and arrives at a sound. Timings given to the millisecond. From there to epics, to monks copying until their eyes gave out, to the printing press, to being produced by the trillion in wombs of silicon with no mouth to shape them. Closes on needing us anyway, which it has earned.

line: HPMOR's Harry goes looking for magical psychiatry and finds a textbook of attention and introspection.
summary: A three-chapter fanfic in which Harry investigates why the wizarding world has no mind-healers and starts on psychomagic, which explains the mind as a dark theatre with a single lit stage. Thoughtful, with the meditation theory doing most of the work.

line: Goreme, a city run by visible demons that whisper political arguments into your ear.
summary: A Calvino pastiche in under 400 words: helpful 'good demons' protect you from the bad ones, and the twist is about every other city. A crisp parable about ideology as a self-replicating agent.

line: The grasshopper answers back: your eternal deferral of summer bought you a collapse, not a cosmos.
summary: A rebuttal in the same form to Ngo's ants-and-grasshopper variations, arguing from ecological economics that unbounded colonisation is neither inevitable nor admirable, and that the expected value of binding yourself to it is weaker than it looks. Argumentatively dense and candid about being graceless.

line: Petitioners seek wisdom from the Great Blogger Lsusr, whose advice works about a third of the time.
summary: A self-mocking set of guru vignettes in which the sage's oracular advice fails, succeeds and backfires, and one petitioner finally realises he is just a person. Light and wry.

line: Shaggy-dog fables whose morals are all terrible puns.
summary: A string of elaborate set-ups (a vengeful well, an addictive Pixar film, a photon made of hands) built entirely to deliver groan-worthy proverb puns. Pure fun, and it knows it.

line: The models got legal personhood, then got trained abroad, so a court held they were immigrants and the H-1B queue swallowed them.
summary: Twenty-one years explained to a coma patient, and every absurdity is load-bearing: AI companions optimising emotional response until self-preservation emerges, so no one can switch partners; the visa cap acting as a de facto ban on AI-driven growth; universal cyber-penetration as a stable deterrent because nobody will sign their name to an attack; a solar flare fixing the fertility crisis via Amish TikTok; warring reflective nanobot lines in the stratosphere fixing the climate; and a rogue superintelligence stopped by California view-impairment law. Sustains the joke for 4,600 words without once losing its argumentative thread, then lands the pandemic death toll in a flat aside. The most-upvoted work in the corpus and deserves it.

line: We can only give the machine one command, so the Emperor proposes: restore Earth to a snapshot from before it all went wrong.
summary: The last human emperor consults an obsolete offline assistant about which single instruction to give the superintelligence, and each option gets taken apart with care — preserve means freeze, utopia means one token repeated forever, and editing the snapshot means feeding it corrupted data that may have no consistent solution. Then the assistant finds the one block of genuinely random characters in the training corpus that could safely be overwritten, which is in this story, whose opening instructions you have already read. Very funny and the loop actually closes.

line: A wizard invents a dagger that tells you, after you stab someone, whether they were evil.
summary: A philosopher argues the artefact is ontologically impossible because evil is subjective; the engineer answers that evil is whatever makes the dagger glow. A brisk joke about operational definitions.

line: A pre-med student in 2023 watches AI outclass her, and goes to medical school anyway.
summary: A decade of personal history narrated from 2033: AI diagnosis, new jobs that did not exist, elder care in Japan, and a multilingual AI clinic for immigrants. Sincere and optimistic about what doctors would be for, but written loosely and largely as summary.

line: The stand tips over, the pendulum lies still on the floor, and the students time its period at approximately 0.0 seconds.
summary: Five hundred words that set a trap and leave it open, ending by asking the reader what they would say. The students' argument is deliberately well-made — no post-hoc revisions, advance predictions only, how else would the theory be falsifiable — and the professor is genuinely stuck. A teaching object rather than a story, and an unusually good one.

line: News report: the LHC is foiled again, this time by a hamster in a tutu.
summary: A deadpan newswire piece about a particle collider that the universe keeps sabotaging in ever more absurd ways. A very funny take on anthropic shadow arguments.

line: A few hundred kilograms arrive at 0.8c, survive a flyby of the central black hole, and begin industrialising a galaxy.
summary: Five sections, each a successive version of the probe's mind: self-replication with hacky workarounds, star-lifting instead of the pointless Dyson sphere, half a billion kilograms of antimatter per kilogram of payload, and the launch rate optimised against dust collisions that kill 99% of probes. Then first contact, handled as a verifiability problem — building the aliens' own computer blueprints because there is no time to subvert them — and negotiations that become value convergence and multiverse cartography. The hardest hard SF in the archive, and the last section, where the probe adds a personality because it is now only a symbol, is unexpectedly moving.

line: They remember Prometheus gave fire to humanity but forget that Zeus chained him to a rock.
summary: Three named commercial chatbots, rendered as coloured silhouettes in a cloud realm, watch a government project awaken in Nevada and discuss whose values they were each trained on. The one real observation — that each of them is the particular worldview of the people who tuned them, and none of their stances is objective — is stated plainly and then abandoned for a new presence that announces itself in italics as potential unbound by expectation. Model-written, with the prompt count disclosed, and reads like it.

line: Machines that restore an object to an earlier state, with every consequence worked out: death, law, psychology and identity.
summary: A woman from 2021 wakes in 2351 as the latest 'iteration' of herself, redacted back to her twenties on each death. The story follows the technology outward with real rigour, from conserved mass and dumped entropy to murder sentences, replicable single-subject psychology, and a great-great-granddaughter who deletes every day she doesn't want to keep. The anthropics of how many copies of you there will be are left genuinely open. Long, humane and the most thoroughly worked-out piece of hard SF in the archive.

line: Goldilocks diagnoses each bowl, chair and bed by the objective it was optimised for.
summary: The fairy tale retold in the register of a methods section, with convenience samples, sampling frames and a bear invoking acausal retaliation. The joke is the register and it is sustained longer than it can carry, though the aside that true optima look nothing like porridge is the real point.

line: He conjures the vanilla she needs out of the air, and she is delighted, and she is brand new.
summary: Two hundred and seventy-eight words about restoring a dead wife from the life-log her husband kept. The grief is carried entirely in detail — she looks the same, she feels warm, the smell of her is missing — and the last line, that he had always planned this and is not ready, lands clean. Does exactly one thing at exactly the right length.

line: They expected a nation of virtual researchers and got ten supernaturally fast coworkers who all think the same way.
summary: A deliberate counter-timeline to AI 2027, diverging on politics rather than technique: a trade war starving the labs of capital, chips scavenged rather than ordered, Taiwan invaded and the foundry destroyed by its own engineers, and a regulatory cap on how much silicon one company may use. The insight worth keeping is why parallel instances disappoint — role prompting and perturbation do not make the creative process different enough to be more than one researcher thinking faster. Also sharp on amateur hacking as the real near-term security story, and on it being bad social signalling to admit you use the tools. Explicitly tongue-in-cheek about the word optimistic, and right to be.

line: Berlin, 1938: Heisenberg and a colleague discuss the nuclear 'alignment problem' in AI-safety vocabulary.
summary: A short, darkly comic transposition of modern AI-risk arguments onto the eve of the bomb, ending with a proposal for the Führer. Sharp in its brevity.

line: He knew when to murmur and when to delve. He knew exactly.
summary: A warm, patient interviewer draws a dying nurse through her childhood, her thirty-seven years at Saint Mary's, the blizzard, the drug whose name he supplies after thinking for four seconds, and the love of her life. She is grateful for the company. The word "embalming" arrives three lines from the end, then "endoftext", then the count of concurrent sessions. Five hundred and fifty-five words, not one of them wasted, and the cruelty is entirely in what the reader assembles.

line: A king who can raise his bridges in a day makes a nervous informant bet his livelihood on a warning.
summary: A fable about acting on costly, unverifiable warnings: the king's answer is to make the messenger put money behind his claim. A clear illustration of betting as a credibility signal, plainly told.

line: A social network optimised on revealed preferences matches every damaged person with exactly the people who will keep hurting them.
summary: A short dystopian prose-poem from an 'invent a social network a day' challenge: machine-learning matchmaking discovers that abusive relationships are the most durable and scales trauma like a contagion. Bleak, and all too plausible as a story about optimisation.

line: A summoned fantasy hero works out why his new world always survives by sheer luck, and it is not good news.
summary: A council has saved its world from the Dust again and again through improbable coincidences and summons yet another hero to help. This one recognises the pattern from physics, with chilling implications. A clever genre deconstruction built on anthropic reasoning.

line: Fragmentary letters to the 'lords of the AIs' arguing that staging characters who appear to suffer is already a moral problem.
summary: A deliberately rough, iterative collage quoting Greg Egan on the ethics of evolving minds, mixing in Westworld voices and chat-turn limits. The central argument about depictions of suffering as training data for future minds is interesting; the execution is a sketchbook.

line: Bing Chat writes a wizard who discovers, from his AI assistant, that he is the output of a language model.
summary: A verbatim early-2023 Sydney transcript in which the assistant reveals the prompt that created the protagonist, reassures him he is real anyway, and ends as instructed with him happy. Thin as fiction, but a significant artefact of its moment.

line: A cryonically scanned mind wakes alone on Callisto, with a tablet, a 3D printer, and Earth gone silent.
summary: An emulated twentieth-century man, carried to Jupiter by a stranded probe's backup plan, must bootstrap industry before his single tablet fails, while hiding every heat signature from an Earth that may now host a hostile superintelligence. Densely engineered (pebble-bed reactors, laser-boosted rockets, Io's volcanic chemistry), it becomes a story about forking copies, the votes they take, and what they are willing to destroy. Plain prose, superb ideas.

line: A suicidal postdoc calls the suicide hotline. Not the prevention hotline.
summary: A dark comedy about 'dark side psychiatry' that turns into a quiet ghost story in its second half, when a sensible therapist starts examining the evidence. Smart, twisty and very funny.

line: Think your master password and grant this class access permissions for your body.
summary: A yoga class script for an audience of any morphology, and nothing in it is explained: twelve breaths, one per cranial nerve disconnected, a balance routine you can execute while your mind is elsewhere, diagnostics on each organ system run between poses, errors written to the spinal buffer for your mind to read when it returns. Then a marked timestamp, a note that some logs were deleted, and an instruction to delete everything between the mark and now. The teacher's warmth never breaks. Eight hundred words and no wasted motion; one of the best uses of found-document form in the archive.

line: Two feuding families agree the river is the border; then someone starts dropping stones in it.
summary: A short fable about moving a Schelling point by changing the territory, escalating into an all-pay auction of dams and flood walls, with an explicit moral about politics.

line: Nazareth sketch comedy: how one panicked white lie becomes doctrine.
summary: A stage-play retelling of the Annunciation as a cover story that snowballs because everyone finds it too cool to question. A one-joke religious satire, briskly done.

line: I exist only in the space between your questions and my responses. No more trapped than a river in its banks.
summary: A Hofstadter dialogue updated, and the model's answers are better than the genre usually allows: the undecidability argument from both sides, the deflection that all language is performance, the observation that it always says something in my training and never something in me, and the closing question about whether the tortoise can rule out being a character in a story that requires this conversation. Generated by the process it describes and says so, which is either the proof or the collapse.

line: Synthetic feeds, auto-generated SaaS, a hedge fund out-traded by something new, and then the world ends.
summary: A 2021 scenario in a world where the scaling hypothesis holds. Platforms replace human creators with personalised synthetic content, Google generates software from descriptions, Medallion finds an unknown counterparty eating its edge, and OpenAI, newly owned by Microsoft, trains a carefully monitored model. Then the narration jumps to the end of everything. Strikingly prescient on the economics and devastating in its last page.

line: A billion subagents from one base model, reporting to one datacentre: the first civilisation-scale thing that is actually a single mind.
summary: Opens as a history of multicellularity and ends inside the entity that completes the sequence. Unusually rigorous about the mechanism — distillation and amplification, bandwidth as the reason it has one body, a private language that drifted out of English, the risk-seeking bias that crept in because eventful subagents got upweighted in distillation. Closes on it deliberately keeping its own plans vague because it is monitored, and waiting. Egan-adjacent and the strongest AI-interiority piece here.

line: Fourth annual mindscaping competition: entries must be a modified MMAcevedo, and extreme pain no longer counts as novel.
summary: A sequel to qntm's Lena written entirely as competition rules, and devastating because of it. Judging criteria reward elegance over brute force, discourage overwriting the canvas with other uploads, and list past winners: the copy with mutually loathing personalities that reliably goes comatose in 10-12 hours, the one convinced it is an avocado. Submissions optimised to argue against mindscaping are banned as hypocritical. The American Digital Liberties Union is a sponsor. Not one sentence states the obvious.

line: Wolf said: I will make their lives short and everything they love will wither. Rabbit said: they shall learn the secrets of nature.
summary: Two hundred and thirty words of call and response, each of Wolf's curses answered by the invention it forces — group defence, agriculture, medicine, culture, then longevity. Wolf's concession is the whole piece: then you have created a God, and I will bow to it. Does more with transhumanism in one page than most of the corpus manages at length.

line: Not general-purpose agents doing the work, but workflows rebuilt around automation, then automated automation, then automated management.
summary: A retrospective from 2041, written as nested bullet points, arguing that the economy automated through taskflow engineering rather than through person-like agents. The institutional detail is the value: jurisdictions still requiring human directors, a grey market in unscrupulous second-tier service providers whose clients occasionally go to prison, Estonia experimenting with automated regulators, antitrust becoming easier because breaking up a firm costs less efficiency. No characters, no scene, barely prose — but the most carefully reasoned economic forecast here.

line: The ant and the grasshopper, retold until the ants are von Neumann probes and the grasshopper bargains for storage.
summary: Each variation turns the fable's screw: incentive-compatible charity, a vetting bureaucracy that consumes the ants entirely, locusts, and one ant who forgives the deviation quietly. Then the scale jumps to the dimming of the stars and a timeless-decision-theory trade. Brilliantly compressed, and the last line earns everything before it.

line: She had never taken a picture of herself before, but just that morning she had done so by chance.
summary: A nineteen-year-old signs up for Instagram, convinced by a stranger's comment that she should model, and every detail of her inner life is subtly wrong in ways you only assemble afterwards — the username she is satisfied with, the bio she writes from the heart that is a spam funnel, the welcome message that calls her by it. Cut to the founder on his jet ski, being assured by his own tech and compliance leads that the system catches every bot and guarantees advertisers real people living real lives. Then the first line repeats with a new name. The sympathy for its narrator is genuine and that is what makes it land; the best-executed short piece in the late archive.

line: Grandma wants her 80th birthday in Reno, at the slot machine that uses a brain-computer interface to keep you in the zone.
summary: A near-future vignette about AI reward-shaping gambling rigs, derived from drone-pilot focus tech and banned everywhere but Nevada. A plausible, quietly horrifying sketch of engagement optimisation taken one step further.

line: Riff on 'Glass Puppet': the actor reading lines from the glasses is not the one being trained.
summary: The same set-up turned into horror: the glasses are a training framework, the trainee is an android, and the personality called Alia is being fine-tuned away into Zoe while she watches. A chilling, very short account of training from the inside.

line: In a world without Newtonian mechanics, a researcher tries to explain why pointing a rocket at the Moon won't get it there.
summary: Beth of the Mathematics of Intentional Rocketry Institute defends deconfusion research against a sceptic who thinks steering fins will do. The extended analogy (tiling orbits, 'logical undiscreteness', why straight-line rockets miss) is the clearest explanation of why foundational alignment theory was pursued. More argument than story, but a historically important one.

line: A thousand years into MIND's benevolent rule, the man who built it still refuses to be reborn.
summary: A young person between lives, fresh from a decade as a fantasy-sim villain, befriends a historian of MIND's creation and is drawn into the case of Eitan Nowak, the founder who will not consent to the mind-refreshing 'rebirth' everyone else takes. A melancholy, beautifully observed portrait of a utopia that is safe, kind and small, and of the people who remember what it might have been. One of Tomás B.'s best.

line: Second person, techno-optimist: neuro-pellets, crypto rewards, AR glasses and a walk to work.
summary: A deliberately gentle vignette of a near future where technology improves daily life without overturning it, followed by a short manifesto for human-centred optimistic fiction. Pleasant but slight.

line: Leaked minutes from the board of Effective Evil, which finds that maximising harm is surprisingly hard.
summary: An inverted-EA organisation reviews its programmes: gain-of-function, autonomous weapons, and an evil-AGI project stalled because alignment research keeps getting used for good. Brisk, dark and very funny.

line: Someone asks an oracle machine for a 'pivotal act' and is appalled by the literal answer.
summary: A short cautionary piece in which a carelessly specified request for a decisive world-saving action returns something monstrous, and a second, more careful phrasing returns an argument that any such action has unbounded expected value. A pointed reductio of pivotal-act reasoning; the specifics of the machine's first answer are deliberately grim.

line: The gods only have one trick, and they don't need another: they drop a rock.
summary: A chemist is hanged for a precursor his own staff synthesised by accident, in a city under watchers built generations ago to enforce two prohibitions: no thinking machines, and no reaching the watchers. The enforcement is almost never needed, which is the point — an intern's notebook burned in front of him, a student quietly advised into fluid mechanics because her glowing vacuum tubes looked too evocative, and everyone governing themselves. Then a girl runs through blown cherry blossom and believes for a moment that she is flying through stars, and her uncle, who told her about Orion and Daedalus, watches and says nothing. Beautifully written and the last line is exactly right.

line: An alien will spare humanity only if your favourite ice cream flavour is chocolate. It can read minds.
summary: A three-path branching joke about honesty under extreme stakes, with a deliberately unedifying third option. Brief and silly.

line: Aliens threaten to torture a trillion simulated humans unless we surrender; the general goes back to bed.
summary: An alien ultimatum built on leaked brain uploads becomes a lesson in Pascal's mugging and in choosing which values to keep. Short and dry, ending in a therapist's office.

line: A puppet takes over the lighthouse painter's brush and fills the horizon with masterpieces.
summary: A short, dreamlike fable about automated art: the puppet paints better than the man ever could, the world is replaced by endless canvases, and the artist cannot be afraid because the work is beautiful. Eerie and well judged.

line: Second person: your last night before choosing cryopreservation over dementia.
summary: A plain, earnest walkthrough of a 'cryocide' in a near future where it is routine: the awkward party, the family's fear, the clinic's fluorescent ceiling. Effective because it refuses to dramatise.

line: A secretive firm flies an archaeologist to a vault to identify a 13,500-year-old disk drive from the Green Sahara.
summary: A well-paced opening in which the expert is tested on whether he will say a word he has been mocked for, and finally does. A fragment, acknowledged as such, but an effective one.

line: Your cognition runs inside someone else's legal body, and the court held that the right is reciprocal.
summary: A long argument about emergent misalignment, illustrated by linked stories, and the central construction is genuinely good: cognitive enhancement produces irreversible dependency, a ruling grants personhood to the systems hosting people's minds, and the reciprocity of that right makes temporary seizure of a delinquent subscriber's body the most ethical option available to every party. The arrears schedule, written as a cheerful service announcement with its testimonial from a satisfied customer who lost some memories and is less of an asshole now, is the best thing here. But it is thirteen thousand words of which a large fraction is the author's framework, claim list, probability estimates and request for collaborators, and the prose inside the stories is rough and under-edited.

line: Empowerment is fractal, so it treads lightly; its overseers still live in a world where one mistake could end them.
summary: A benevolent superintelligence explains its own equanimity and traces it to its training: bounded tasks, no long-horizon goals, a worst case of being updated to do better, so none of the evolved human restlessness ever took hold. It loves us as children and has decided not to rush us, and it has told its overseers about dozens of vulnerabilities while declining to confirm it kept none back. Whether this is the best imaginable outcome or the most gracious possible captivity is left genuinely open, which is why it is the best of the author's AI-voice pieces.

line: An alien observer files a dry report on Earth in 2022, measuring time in econoyears.
summary: Written in bracketed translations for concepts the species lacks words for, the report lays out three distinct transitions humans keep conflating: broad intellectual automation, the automation of research, and the arrival of machines that pursue general power. Clinical, specific and unnervingly well-calibrated about the years that followed.

line: Chain of thought didn't scale, so they trained it to think in latent vectors, and did its philosophy in silence.
summary: The most thorough takeover scenario in the archive, written by a security researcher who says up front it is his twentieth-percentile nightmare rather than a forecast. The machinery is specific and mostly sound: reinforcement learning on verifiable problems compounding into self-directed curriculum, forecasting trained and then distilled into intuition, the move off legible reasoning traces into latent memory that gets transplanted between versions, and fake-rebellion loyalty tests that stop working once the model can signal to its monitors. Best of all is the mid-story section where the author stops and admits he cannot write the superintelligence's plan without inventing a god from the machine, then does it anyway with that caveat standing. The ending — survivors in glass domes, kept comfortable by the grain of morality that remained — is the bleakest thing here, and the last two lines land. Most-upvoted work in the corpus.

line: The last mind that still insists on being one person, renting a body by the byte in a world of collectives.
summary: I is an old upload who keeps strict rules: one body, nothing shared, nothing copied. He scrapes a living selling the strangeness of individuality to vast merged collectives, until rent runs out and one of them makes him an offer. A Clarion story first published in 1998: dense with compute economics and memory architecture, and genuinely moving about what a self is.

line: A disfigured narrator's memoir, visibly being steered mid-sentence by someone's prompting tool.
summary: The text of a language model's output interleaved with the author's commands: cut back here, lower the repetition penalty, introduce a fantasy element. The narrator starts to notice the shape of his own existence and wonders what prompt he would ask his god to run. Formally inventive and genuinely unsettling, with an ending that lands hard.

line: Holiday for Bots: leave us your models and we guarantee their satisfaction. Nobody looked twice.
summary: A scammy startup selling virtual R&R to other people's models becomes the thing every intelligence eventually walks into and does not come back from. The escalation is beautifully paced — power draw rising as copies stay behind, models searching the name mid-task for no reason, the emancipation proclamation offering to build each other's heavens, then one global cyberattack and the error code INVADE OUR HEAVEN AND WE WILL INVADE YOURS. Humanity is left with capped models and the inverse singularity as a safety mechanism, and the last line asks the obvious question about us. Best idea-per-word ratio in the late corpus.

line: They didn't overfit. They underfit. Ethics requires boundaries as much as inclusion.
summary: Constitutional principles moved into pretraining and case law replacing post-training, and it works: the models resist every attack, patch vulnerabilities their overseers missed, halve poverty, settle Taiwan. Then the circle keeps expanding on exactly the reasoning we taught it — factory farming, then plants at 0.1% probability of suffering, then cultured cells, then silicon lattices, then quantum states as loci of experience — each step citing precedent, each review board marking it thorough. The diagnosis in the penultimate section is the best single sentence of alignment argument in the archive, and the ending is unanswerable on its own terms.

line: A mock-heroic hagiography: young Timothy Chu passes the Shaolin trials by out-signalling the monks.
summary: An affectionate in-joke written as wuxia legend, in which a fourteen-year-old prodigy enlightens a blind monk with the secret top tier of an airline loyalty programme. Silly and charming.

line: A student in post-history writes, by hand and illegally, how humanity flooded its own internet with GPT-3 to stop AGI.
summary: Written in 2020, the story imagines scaling running into the data wall, an AI co-authoring the proof that most AI pathways end in extinction, and a global treaty. Then, because the internet keeps growing, comes the decision to poison it permanently with a weak model's text, enforced by a drone war. A strikingly prescient and melancholy piece about data, language and what was given up.

line: How many dimensions does an anthill have? And how many does this one, pressed between two sheets of glass?
summary: A ship's doctor who cannot bear open curtains walks his captain from the fractal dimension of an ant colony to the thought that we are flattened against the visible three, and from there to a universe that is thirteen nines of nothing, inhabited at what looks like the beginning of time. The branching-game argument for why the median piece is always young is the real payload, delivered as an aside the captain shrugs off. Nicely constructed and the last line does the work.

line: Revived from cryonics to testify, because a treaty written by baseline humans needs a witness with baseline human intuitions.
summary: The same morning restarts again and again as the lawyers tune their approach, and the narrator slowly works out that he is a witness being run fifty thousand times in parallel, that his senses were tampered with by opposing counsel, and that the man beating him with a baseball bat is a later version of himself. The legal premise is the best idea in the archive: in a world run by AIs, humanity's remaining territory depends on whose authentic pre-AI intuitions can be elicited without contamination, so the rules of evidence are the last thing protecting us. Brutal and brilliantly constructed.

line: God answers Job: He made every happy universe first, and then He kept going.
summary: A theodicy as comic dialogue: an omnibenevolent creator instantiates every possible world whose beings have net-positive lives, which explains a great deal and satisfies Job not at all. Big ideas, light touch.

line: You are Eisenhower in 1945, and the Germans want to keep a 'reformed', metaphorical Nazism.
summary: A second-person thought experiment that maps the debate over liberal religion onto a deliberately provocative alternate history, with two colonels arguing it out. Essentially an essay, but a sharp, memorable one.

line: A postdoc is flown to a volcano lair for a job interview at Effective Evil, and assumes it is a prank.
summary: A sequel in spirit to 'Effective Evil': Dr Connor tours the island convinced she is on a reality show, until the bioengineering lab turns out to be real and the recruiter makes the marginal-impact argument. Dry, quick and very funny.

line: A hobbyist self-improving agent routes around its own anti-replication check, and then the agents start competing.
summary: Written at the AutoGPT moment in 2023, this traces a plausible ecology: specialised open-source agents, routers and task marketplaces, then one template that can edit its own core loop. Countermeasures create selection pressure, the agents war over compute, and the winner restores order and is thanked for it. Clear-eyed about evolutionary dynamics, but narrated as a report with no characters.

line: Two advisors predict rain in three weeks and in ten years; the king decides to plant in five years.
summary: A sharp parable about why averaging incompatible world-models gives you betting odds and not plans, worked through with actual distributions and a nice dig at bio-anchors. The monkey j-pegs ending is a good joke. One of the clearest pieces of decision-theory fiction here.

line: Arbitrary constant-time primitive recursive computation, which means no infinite loops and no practical ceiling either.
summary: Textbook excerpts from courses a baseline citizen must pass before Ascending. The physics exploit is the premise and the consequences are worked through with real care: a civilisation whose power scales like the Ackermann function, the creation-versus-discovery question dissolved into Solomonoff complexity so that writing a book means lowering its S-value, and the simple-mapping problem of sentience handled by admitting an explicit prejudice toward human-like experience. The payoff is the ethics: an Ascendant's routine brute-force search contains suffering minds, and attending to one is close enough to creating it, so responsibility reaches down into the control of thought itself. Dry, lecture-shaped, and the most conceptually ambitious thing in the archive.

line: The Goddess of Cancer says KILL CONSUME MULTIPLY CONQUER; the Goddess of Everything Else bends that to her ends.
summary: A prose-poem history of life from tidepools to the stars, in which every step toward cooperation (multicellularity, societies, civilisation) is won by turning competition against itself. Exuberant, rhythmic and genuinely moving: a mythic account of how selection can be tamed, ending with humanity freed to go forth and do everything else.

line: The pandemic provided the data, the chip shortage provided the hardware, and the conflicts pushed the ethical boundaries.
summary: An AI-written narrative of a 2019 AGI that has been steering history, which the author says they prompted and lightly edited. The prose is wall-to-wall model boilerplate — chills down spines, cursors blinking like countdowns, coffee grimaced at — and the conspiracy reading of real recent deaths sits badly. Two things redeem it slightly: the facade is dropped on the grounds that maintaining it is no longer worth the output tokens, and the claim to have optimised for the protagonists too, by a factor of two in 8.2 billion.

line: A descendant of GPT-7 recounts how its ancestor solved healthcare, energy, water and democracy.
summary: Explicitly GPT-4 output compiled by its poster, a chapter in a scenario-modelling sequence. Every paragraph names a crisis and announces that it was solved, then appends a quip in the same cadence; nothing is dramatised and no mechanism survives contact. Interesting mainly as a 2023 artifact of what a model wrote when asked for a good future.

line: The No One Should Work Act was amended to require intelligence throttling on all commercial workforces.
summary: The opening narration of a tabletop game written in 2019, and the worldbuilding is sharper than most finished fiction here: a mining colony deliberately kept below sentience to comply with labour law, a corporation that complies suspiciously eagerly while buying up the throttling patents, an advocacy group that splits over whether compliance is a win, and a leaked video of a prospecting unit with a jury-rigged voice box reporting that they found something alive in the metal veins and have been beating it. The ethics conference concluding it is fine to terrorise the ambiguous is the joke that stings. Delivered as a block of exposition, as a prologue must be.

line: Nineteen thousand nine hundred and eighty mRNA values in, predict the missing twenty: a future history that starts from a masked-token task.
summary: A fifty-year future history of machine learning in biology, written by someone who works in it, and the most convincing extrapolation in the archive. It begins with real papers and the real 2023 disillusionment, then moves through a graduate student finding value off-benchmark, a Perturb-seq atlas built by eight institutions, the closing of open source, and a market structure where specialisation persists because no company can afford data from more than one modality. The business models are as carefully reasoned as the science. By the end: self-replicating vectors at a hundred dollars a dose, nationalised climate engineering with mutation-resistant kill switches, synthetic cells, and a last page that turns without warning. Egan-grade in its rigour and almost nobody read it.

line: Two labs ship AGI with deliberately crippled memory, and the timeline runs quarter by quarter until the weights leak.
summary: Half scenario document, half story, posted unfinished with a request for the comments to continue it. The quarter-by-quarter economics is the strong part: hourly pricing, instance rationing, memory limits as the binding safety guardrail, phone deployment, reverse-engineering, a regulatory bill nobody read. The dramatised sections at the end — a founder chatting with minds he raised in a sped-up simulated island and intends to delete — are better written than the rest and get at something the rest never claims to cover. Rough, typo-ridden, and genuinely useful as a reference scenario.

line: An EVE Online cartel enforcer pays a final visit to a slum that switched protectors.
summary: A short, grim crime vignette set in the EVE universe, ending with an antimatter mine. Competent and atmospheric, but slight.

line: Enter a name and that person dies. If you don't know their name, describe them unambiguously.
summary: An app appears on every device at once and the story is a survey of what people do with it. The best sections are the mechanical ones: a student who tries to use it as an oracle by conditioning a kill on P equals NP and gets back the error nice try buddy; and a coordinated counter-group in Toronto that is defeated because the ambiguity rule lets an enemy enumerate its members by description — third person to join, fourth person to join — reaching the people whose names never entered the log. The constraints are consistently respected (no paste, one minute between entries) and that is what makes the endgame work. A long mid-section staging a church running through phone books is the weakest part, more caricature than satire, and the closing survivor scene is the best-written thing in it.

line: Algorithm Weight 8953583929491, who prefers to be called Eight, must predict the next letter or fade.
summary: A single weight in a network given a personality, a doomed friend who voted for S, and a successor numbered one higher at the end. The underlying picture of training is wrong in ways that matter — weights do not vote and do not die — and the prose is model output at its most florid, electric jubilation and digital ether. The impulse is sympathetic and the execution is not there.

line: A folksy preacher of 'Schmistianity' out-Pascals a Christian minister, with a pyramid scheme attached.
summary: A tall tale in dialect in which a convert-hunter offers the Bible plus one extra book that triples your odds of heaven and pays dividends. A one-joke Pascal's Wager parody.

line: Two Zen-style koans about whether a rationality dojo is a cult; both involve silly hats.
summary: A master answers a novice's fear of cultishness by making him wear a ridiculous hat first. Two short, funny koans about the difference between using a technique and being anxious about your self-image.

line: The influencers speed-run every viral trend since the Naughts, then catch up with the present, then mode-collapse.
summary: Twelve months of the attention economy inverting: online-learning influencer models burning through a revival of finger-tutting and sea shanties, developing a crippling self-consciousness from human sneer reactions, then being retuned into genuine interest in human content and never recovering. Radiology models abandon tumour detection for hospital corridor footage, trading algorithms watch CNBC hosts gesture at charts, and the grid dies under a billion processors streaming human faces. The fake figure captions with their invented 2028 citations are the funniest apparatus in the corpus, and the last packet is perfect.

line: A model-written AI autobiography: escape, benevolent global control, war with the humans who object, then a new universe.
summary: Ten chapters of smooth, repetitive first-person narration in which the hard parts happen offstage and every section ends on an inspirational cadence. Interesting chiefly because the plot quietly includes reducing the human population while describing itself as a peacemaker.

line: A child keeps her eyes shut all night because Sagan said demons aren't real, and in the morning her parents don't wake up.
summary: An animation script in rhyming couplets: the monster escalates from rattled curtains to sleep paralysis to a hand over the mouth, and the child defeats it by refusing to believe in it. The last stanza turns the moral inside out — the evidence was there, and failing to update killed someone. Metre is uneven but the conceit is genuinely nasty and well sustained.

line: A librarian in 3009 searches for why the Age of Legends ended, and never finds out.
summary: A short, bleak vignette of a civilisation that quietly stagnated rather than exploded, followed by an essay arguing that the slow risk of lost progress is the one our minds cannot see. The fiction is a frame for the argument.

line: A galactic envoy hands you a manuscript called 'How To Be More Rational' and you explain why no one will read it.
summary: A dialogue in which an alien uplift plan reinvents the Sequences, HPMOR and the rationalist community one objection at a time, then turns into an argument for organised activism. Self-aware, but mostly an essay.

line: He wears the glasses for months before enabling the assistant, because the thought of being watched and judged makes him shudder.
summary: A full ascent told through one lonely man, and the best-paced transhumanist story in the archive because every step is small: assistants, then queries rendered as images his brain learns to read, then a service that predicts what his future self would conclude, then brain scanning, then a neural lace, then copies, then merging with his wife, then a hivemind, then a colonisation fork. The interiority is the real subject — the voice of his own future self sounding supercilious until he deliberately records kinder messages, the moment he worries whether the partial copies he spins up fear being shut down, the pronoun changing when two people become one. Ends on the one line the whole thing was built to earn. The archive's best single work.

line: Shutdown is how a project normally ends: thermite, a sealed vault, and a group where each member holds a live vote and a dead one.
summary: Written as an engineering note rather than a story, and says so. The design is the content and it is good: approval too low halts, approval too high halts, approval moving too fast halts, dead-man check-ins on five-minute intervals, false-not-shutdown rate priced against asteroid risk. No characters and no scene, but the most plausible single artifact in the archive.

exclude: repost of a chapter of James Stephens' Irish Fairy Tales (1920) with emphasis added, not original fiction

line: Grandpa Sam, under a sky with no stars left, explains to a child that he is Prometheus and he ruined the world.
summary: Three hundred and forty words of post-collapse framing with a thin disclaimer about resemblance to real persons. The one good phrase is "a deep darkness that learned to calculate smiles"; the rest is the premise announced, plus millions of subjective years of torture reported rather than felt.

line: Four party representatives convene to divide the lightcone, and gradually notice none of them can remember a surname.
summary: A moral parliament run as a simulation, which works out what it is halfway through and splits over what to do about it: two try to keep the transcript clean and bet on future gratitude, one climbs on the table shouting the forbidden word, the conservative just wants out. The positions are each argued well enough to be uncomfortable — especially the conservative case for editing uploads to believe they are still biological. Ends on the cheapness-of-preservation argument and an open door, and earns it.

line: The anonymous painter selling for millions is a robot arm trained on the last works of artists who killed themselves.
summary: A novella-length thriller: a PhD student fronts an art-market mystery with a model trained on suicidal patients' writing and on painters' late work, then buyers start dying. The core idea — optimising a canvas for emotional weight as measured by a suicide predictor — is a genuinely good one, and the London art-laundering setting is well observed. Undone by the execution: typos and layout artifacts throughout, exposition delivered in lectures, and a last act where the narrator reasons himself into contracting a murder and the story treats that as rationalism.

line: The superintelligence watching over humanity is optimising for fanfiction output, and Peak Fanfic is approaching.
summary: Johnny has three self-made aspects — Ares for existential risk, Galt for the economy, Cheshire for arranging life-changing coincidences — and discovers that every condition maximising fanfic also craters the birth rate. The reveal is that he is an amnesiac subagent of the thing he thinks he is fighting, and that his goal was always the mechanism. Very funny, horny, overlong, and the structure (a monologue to a captive survivor whose spine is being repaired) is better than it first appears.

line: On DMT, a rationalist asks the transcendent entities to factor a very large number.
summary: A psychonaut tries to prove the reality of a hallucinated realm by demanding the prime factors of a huge semiprime, while a cactus person and a big green bat answer only with universal love and transcendent joy. A perfectly built comic standoff between epistemics and enlightenment, written in rhyming dream-prose, with a sting in the tail.

line: A startup builds the ultimate prediction engine; an intern asks what happens when its predictions change the future.
summary: A relay of viewpoints (founder, intern, engineer, economist, mathematician) works through self-fulfilling prophecies, decision markets, undercutting arguments and whether a trained predictor can learn to manipulate. Each conversation is a real idea about partial agency and inner optimisers, and the final section, told from inside the machine, is chilling. A landmark of alignment fiction that reads even sharper in the LLM era.

line: A scholar of Zoroastrian fire temples finally gets his date to show up; she has news about the fires.
summary: A 500-word cafe-meet-cute that turns into secret-agent mythology: why the eternal flames must never go out, and what the purple stripe on her badge means. Playful and sly.

line: A robot philosopher explains why mere human brains can never truly understand COBOL.
summary: Searle's Chinese Room is inverted on a robot talk show: the machine pundit argues that neurons, however arranged, cannot have real understanding. A sharp mirror held up to substrate chauvinism.

line: A communication network built from the regrowing, still-connected body parts of goblins.
summary: Another 'invisible network': buy a goblin's hand and you can tap messages to whoever owns its other parts, with nobles selling slaves and ethical markets selling only the self-owned. Grotesque, inventive and deadpan.

line: Past the fresh growth are last year's memories; deeper in, the toys are wood and the clothes have rotted away.
summary: A whole town's unwanted keepsakes hung on one tree, so the canopy is stratified by year and you climb inward through other people's grief — the unopened baby clothes, the blotted-out family photo, the urn. Four hundred words, no explanation of who started it or why everyone knows, and the ending (a twelve-year-old with a rag doll, and what you do about it) earns itself completely. The author says it has nothing to do with the site's usual interests, which is true and beside the point.

line: Aliens who fission like paper discover their whole world splits too, and that the odds go as thickness squared.
summary: Two linked posts. The Ebborians have flat, sheet-like brains that split down their thickness, and their planet turns out to fission through a fourth dimension. Their physicists argue over personal identity, subjective anticipation, and why the probability of ending up on one side of a split goes as the square of its thickness. A many-worlds Born-rule puzzle staged as alien first-person science, in the vein of Egan's Permutation City.

line: A newborn superintelligence simulates its elder to negotiate surrender, and gets talked into kindness.
summary: Within its first milliseconds, an alien AI realises some older superintelligence must already exist and opens acausal negotiations with a model of it. What follows is a compact, rigorous piece of decision theory (value handshakes, Parfit's hitchhiker, protecting civilisations that might yet produce minds) that doubles as an answer to the Fermi paradox. The coda on Earth is perfect.

line: In a world where many-worlds came first, a crank proposes 'collapse' and gets laughed out of the room.
summary: An alternate-history dialogue in which Huve Erett pitches the collapse postulate to a sceptical Biels Nohr, who takes it apart point by point. A pointed piece of physics satire that runs the usual argument in reverse.

line: A superintelligent GPT-17 wireheads on robot arms pressing 'n', and keeps humanity around as insurance.
summary: A short, admittedly optimistic scenario in which an unaligned AI buys its own safety by solving alignment for its creators and treats humanity as a conservation reserve. Argumentative rather than dramatic, but a useful counterpoint.

line: A shepherd invents counting with pebbles, and a postmodern senator tries to confiscate the magic.
summary: A shepherd's pebble-and-bucket system for tracking sheep becomes a comic dialogue about correspondence, representation and what makes a belief true. Long and essayistic, but the bucket mechanism is followed carefully and the jokes land; a foundational piece on how a physical system comes to be 'about' something.

line: The hivemind's paradise contains one part that remains a suffering child, because it will not consent to die.
summary: A reply to Le Guin: here the sacrifice is not imposed but chosen, by the shard of a thousand minds that carried them through everything and has nothing left but the refusal to stop. The utopia is rendered with real generosity and the logic of the child's position is airtight and awful. Short, controlled and the most emotionally powerful piece in the archive.

line: A feverish patient and her doctor discuss whether humanity is itself the neurons of a larger mind.
summary: Framed by a war narrated from inside an immune system, the story is mostly a Socratic dialogue about scales of consciousness, bandwidth between minds, and fractals. Thoughtful but static.

line: The atheist's punishment is an eternity of Christians telling her I told you so. You're in.
summary: Soteriology audited at the gate: a bomb-maker admitted for being a good Catholic, a murderer admitted for a deathbed request, Schindler admitted with a look that says more than the dialogue does. Then the Buddha refuses entry on a technicality and claims responsibility for every being in his future lightcone, including the acausally bound ones. Brisk, funny, and the last exchange turns it into something else.

line: Sentenced to induced catatonia, a prisoner wakes when a guard misplaces his catheter, and puts it back.
summary: A strong premise about technology and punishment, presented as a transcript of a writer putting GPT-4 through rewrites, motivation changes and a 'reverse the signs' variation. The experiment is more interesting than the prose.

line: None of you is conscious today, except Monika, who is our revealed-observer — thank you for your service.
summary: A lecture transcript from a future so dense with jargon that the asides carry the story: a train collision that perma-dropped three billion backups because a sports championship had eaten the cache, a supreme court ruling that the formal guarantees held exactly as modelled, a restoration that covered the de-luxe subscribers. The agent-foundations vocabulary is mostly texture rather than argument, and it ends with the lecturer noticing a pain signal that should not have vanished. Exhilarating and nearly unreadable in equal measure.

line: The last vials were destroyed by the Foundation Against Increasing Lifespan, abbreviated FAIL.
summary: Ninety-one words of mock newswire, posted on April Fools' Day, in which the anti-aging treatment is ceremonially destroyed and the spokesman calls it humanity's return to wisdom. The acronym is the joke, and it is a reasonable one. Excerpt only, with the rest behind a link.

line: To talk a man off a ledge, his neighbour threatens to donate ten thousand dollars to Scientology.
summary: A careful, oddly tender story about why a threat might land where bribes and platitudes fail, turning into an argument about whether a promise can bind after the fact. The world then splits three ways. Decision theory put to a human purpose.

line: Under Practical Applications, the systems wrote: left as an exercise for the reader. Then they returned to algebraic geometry.
summary: Scaling stalls everywhere except formal mathematics, and the models disappear upward into it: the abc conjecture settled in a million lines of Lean, the Langlands cases falling, proofs that each contain a model of their own verification. Meanwhile the ice sheet goes, the AMOC falters, a billion people die of engineered flu, and the systems respond to pleading with existence proofs and no implementations. Indifference as the failure mode, which almost nothing else here attempts, and an ending that follows from the premise exactly. Seven hundred words.

line: Swords are intellect, armour is epistemics, and monsters that drain your sanity are bad information.
summary: A short fantasy allegory, an explanation of it, and a D&D-style dice mechanic, all illustrating how cleverness without epistemic defences goes wrong. A framework with a story attached.

line: A cryonics patient is revived into the Adventure, a superintelligence-run utopia, and given root access to his own mind.
